full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT.** Polar order arising when agents turn away from each other is documented. But this run's mix of strong polar order and strong clumping contradicts what that literature reports. My best guess is that this is a numerical artifact, though I couldn't confirm that from the literature.

**What's documented**
- Das et al. (PRX 14, 031008, 2024) show that flocking can also emerge through interactions that turn agents away from each other. In their account, the polar state is stable because particles achieve a compromise between turning away from left and right neighbors.
- A related mechanism in phoretic colloids: a flocking transition mechanism... sustained purely by chemo-repulsive torques at low to medium densities (Subramaniam et al., Soft Matter 2025).
- The rule itself is essentially the "zone of repulsion" rule from Couzin-type models (move directly away from neighbours, plus noise), with no zone of orientation or attraction. Romenskyy & Lobaskin used that rule together with alignment. There, repulsion did not create order: at high density it caused a transition into a disordered phase... attributed to the destructive action of the repulsions.

**The twist, and why it matters**
1. **There is no separate push between agents.** Das et al. stress that unlike for alignment interactions, the emergence of polar order from turn-away interactions requires particle repulsion. Their mechanism is that repulsion... pushes particles out of the interaction range before they have time to turn completely. Here the turn is instant and complete, so that mechanism doesn't straightforwardly apply. The first pass treated the two systems as equivalent without checking this.
2. **Strong clumping goes against the literature.** Das et al. report that turn-away interactions hinder the formation of polar clusters, as particles at the cluster edge turn away and move into low-density areas. At high density they find flocking Wigner crystals, i.e. evenly spaced lattices, not clumps. Cell models of turning away from contact likewise show that this yields an effective repulsion that promotes cell dispersal. If a nearest-neighbour ratio of 0.1 really means typical nearest-neighbour distances about a tenth of random, a repulsion-only rule is producing stacked agents. That matters a lot: it would be either a new effect or, more likely, a bug.

**Why I lean towards artifact**
- At this density (400 agents in 400 units² of area, interaction radius 1.5), almost every agent has a neighbour in range at every step. So headings are almost always reset from neighbour positions rather than persisting, and it's unclear what would sustain real polar order.
- Polar order and stacking appearing together is a classic sign of a degenerate case: overlapping agents with an undefined "away" direction (e.g. atan2(0,0)=0) all heading the same way. Large fixed steps (0.3) with nearest-only reactions could also cause leapfrogging.
- The metric scales are unclear. "Higher = stronger" next to "below 1 = clustered" contradict each other, so 0.1 might not be a raw ratio.

**Checks to run:** a histogram of headings (a spike at 0 rad would suggest an artifact); the fraction of agent pairs closer than 0.01; behaviour as the step size shrinks; and averaging over all neighbours in range instead of only the nearest.

**Searches run:** Flocking by Turning Away; turn-away/nearest-neighbour repulsion with polar order; Vicsek-type models with repulsion only; phoretic repulsive-torque flocking; flocking with purely repulsive point particles; Couzin repulsion zone only; Romenskyy–Lobaskin; contact-inhibition-of-locomotion models. I did not read the Baconnier et al. self-aligning review (RMP 2025) in full.
